summary:
Sarawak stands under Malaysia's national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; the provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Acts of gross indecency are separately punishable. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Sarawak is one of the 13 states whose Sharia enactments criminalise cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim visitor is not exposed to that layer; enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded. There is no same-sex marriage and no federal law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Documented enforcement since the 2018 election has been raid-based and public. An October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur produced at least 20 arrests of LGBT people, and an August raid on an LGBT venue detained twenty men. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022: media were pre-tipped, detainees' faces and personal details were leaked, 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended, a magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, and more than 130 people were held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. A further sauna raid followed in Penang days later.

Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. The audited sources record no Sarawak-specific enforcement case, so the national pattern is what a visitor here should expect.

Trans people in Malaysia also face lethal violence. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.
tangentialFactors:
Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional; the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Official hostility has been stated openly. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled abroad and received UNHCR protection.

Adjacent measures indicate the direction of policy. A Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned, and in November 2023 Johor announced plans for conversion-therapy centres. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, LGBT events and media content are censored, and Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects.

On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister floated revisiting the sauna-raid provisions, a step Justice For Sisters had supported by mobilising bailors and legal aid during the detentions.
localsOnly:
Sarawak's Sharia enactments bind Muslim residents: cross-dressing and posing as a woman are state offences punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a RM5,000 fine and six strokes of caning, investigated and enforced by the state Islamic religious department rather than the police. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men.

Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no access to same-sex marriage. A dual court system applies Sharia jurisdiction to Muslims only, while the Penal Code reaches everyone.

A Human Rights Watch report published on 10 August 2022, drawing on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021, documents state religious authorities harassing LGBT activists and organisations, raiding private events, and running government "rehabilitation" programmes that at least 1,733 people had attended as of June 2021. The report also records conversion practices as a lived reality for residents, not only an announced policy.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Sarawak-specific enforcement case appears in the audited sources. Whether Sarawak has prosecuted cross-dressing offences, and how often, is unresolved in this record; the national enforcement pattern is used as the working expectation.

Whether Sarawak's enactment also bars women from posing as men is not sourced. Three states are recorded as doing so, but which three is not stated in the inventory.

The August raid on an LGBT venue is dated only to August, with the year and location not specified in the source claim, and the 20 arrested are described as men; whether any were transgender is unresolved.

The status after late 2014 of the constitutional challenge filed after the mass arrest of 16 trans women is not sourced, and the outcome of the Home Minister's December 2025 suggestion to revisit section 377B is likewise unresolved.

Whether the 2022 Human Rights Watch report contains Sarawak-specific findings is not identified in the inventory; only its federation-wide conclusions are recorded here.
